newsitem.title: ERITREA: Sudan rebels say they capture another garrison.
newsitem.headline: Sudan rebels say they capture another garrison.

text.p: The Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) said on Wednesday a joint rebel force had captured another Sudanese army garrison northeast of the town of Kassala as Khartoum declared an Islamic "holy war" to counter advancing rebels.

A spokesman for John Garang, head of the SPLA and chairman of a joint rebel military command, told Reuters that the rebels, operating under the umbrella National Democratic Alliance, captured the garrison at Gadamyeeb at noon on Tuesday. He said the rebels were attacking other garrisons in the same area.
Kassala is close to the Eritrean border and lies about 280 miles (450 km) east of the Sudanese capital.
The SPLA has been fighting in the southern Sudan since 1983 but the rebel movement suffered setbacks when it splintered in 1991.
But it has since recovered, thanks to a military and political alliance with northern opposition groups based in the Eritrean capital.

"The chairman of the Joint Military Command, John Garang, has announced that our forces captured Gadamyeeb, an army garrison and village northeast of Kassala from NIF (government) forces yesterday (Tuesday) at noon," the spokesman said.
He said rebel forces were also attacking the garrison at Koteneb in the same area and others were attacking the strategic town of Maban, where heavy fighting was taking place.

The rebels have already seized two towns on the border with Ethiopia -- Kurmuk and Qeissan, about 600 km (370 miles) southeast of Khartoum -- and on Monday they captured key army garrisons at Al-Kali, Daimonsour and Shali al-Fil in the southern Blue Nile region.
Sudan has accused Ethiopia and Eritrea of invading Africa's biggest nation and coordinating the rebel attacks. All two countries have denied involvement.
Sudanese military ruler President Omar Hassan al-Bashir has called for general mobilisation against the threat, which includes sending university students to the front.
Sudanese radio reported on Tuesday that Bashir said Sudan would wage "jihad" -- Islamic holy war -- against what he called Ethiopian aggression.
In a report monitored by the British Broadcasting Corporation, Bashir, who is a devolut Moslem, said the battle was now with "the enemies of the faith and of the homeland".
Political and diplomatic channels had been closed and the only route left was the power of the gun, said the lieutenant-general who seized power in a coup in 1989.
